
=================================================================
#49 Royal Secretariat  (651)
Arc: The Chunchu Era · tone: statecraft drama
Logline: One seal. One speed. Fewer uncles.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ For three months a border petition has been circling the **Harmony Council** like a bird that cannot find a roof. Chunchu has counted the seals. He has counted the men who must touch a paper before a soldier may move. He has stopped counting aloud, because the room mistakes counting for patience.
[1] ¶ He has reasons to be in a hurry. The emperor who promised him an army, in a gallery of stone horses, has been dead two years. The promise went into the tomb with him, or near enough.
[2] ¶ He clears a side hall in the palace — small enough that the old clans will call it irregular, large enough for the work. Three clerks. One courier captain. A table that has never held a feast. He practices the sentence the way other men practice a sword form.
[3] King Muyeol: A petition.
[4] King Muyeol: A seal.
[5] King Muyeol: A courier.
[6] King Muyeol: Are you getting it?
[7] King Muyeol: These are not three separate offices.
[8] King Muyeol: This is one office.
[9] King Muyeol: We call it the Royal Secretariat.
[10] King Muyeol: Today, Silla reinvents the court.
[11] ¶ Nobody laughs. The youngest clerk writes the name down as if the words had always been waiting for ink. Outside, the Harmony Council is still debating the same petition. Inside, the petition has somewhere to land.
[12] [CARD Kim Jukji: A Hwarang who sailed with Chunchu to Chang’an and wrote down everything. Quiet, exact, and always holding the right paper.]
[13] Kim Jukji: Petition. Seal. Courier. / I can do that before the Council finishes clearing its throat.
[14] King Muyeol: Then you are its Premier. The Secretariat is yours. / You’re young, you’re quick, and you already write faster than the Council talks. / In Chang’an the emperor does not wait for every uncle to agree. I watched that power and wanted it for this country — not for my vanity. For speed.
[15] ¶ The Council finds out in the third week. Alchun is High Councillor now, because after Bidam nobody else wanted the chair. He comes to the side hall himself, with the border petition under his arm. He has been meaning to debate it.
[16] Alchun: Oi. This petition. / We were going to argue about it at the full moon.
[17] Kim Jukji: It’s sealed, my lord. The garrison marched yesterday.
[18] Alchun: Yesterday. / …Then what’s the Council for, Chunchu?
[19] King Muyeol: For the day the seal is wrong, my lord. / Somebody has to be in the room to say so.
[20] Alchun: …That’s a very polite way of saying a chair.
[21] ¶ He leaves the petition on the table anyway, sealed, like a man returning a borrowed bowl.
[22] ¶ In the market a storyteller invents a joke that sticks: _Our prince is in love with the emperor._ Another version: _enamored with China._ Chunchu hears both and does not correct them. Munhee, packing a different set of bags, corrects them for him.
[23] Munhee: He is in love with a door that opens when he knocks. / Call that China if you like. I call it not waiting for twelve men to finish a sentence.
[24] Kim Jukji: The Council asked what my title means. / I told them: 侍中 — I stand beside the work. / They did not laugh. That was how I knew it had worked.
[25] ── SCENE: Tang Dress ──
[26] ¶ What Chunchu brought home from Chang’an fits on one sheet. Jukji reads it out at the Secretariat table. Chunchu answers before he reaches the end of each line.
[27] Kim Jukji: First, address. In Chang’an only the emperor is “Your Majesty.” / So Her Majesty becomes “Your Highness.”
[28] King Muyeol: Then she is Your Highness. A word is a cheap coat. / Let them see us wearing it.
[29] Kim Jukji: Second, the years. Taehwa is retired. From now on we count Yonghui. / The emperor’s years.
[30] King Muyeol: Taehwa. “Great Harmony.” A fine name. It never harmonised anything. / Retire it with honours.
[31] Kim Jukji: Third, dress. Tang robes and caps for every official, an ivory tablet in every hand. / I once saw a camel driver in Chang’an better turned out than our whole—
[32] King Muyeol: Officials. Only officials.
[33] Kim Jukji: …And the people?
[34] King Muyeol: The people keep their own clothes. / If the whole market starts dressing like Chang’an, someone in Chang’an will think he owns the market.
[35] Kim Jukji: Fourth. Chang’an asks, very politely, about our borders. Tribute. Garrisons—
[36] King Muyeol: We send silk and poems. We keep the country. / Write it so they can’t tell which one I said louder.
[37] Kim Jukji: Fifth, the crowns. A court in Tang dress, they say, should not be seen in—
[38] King Muyeol: No.
[39] Kim Jukji: I haven’t finished the—
[40] King Muyeol: The crowns stay. Have you looked at them? Gold trees. Antlers. Little jade commas that ring when you nod. / The emperor can have our calendar. He can’t have those.
[41] ¶ Jukji writes every answer down. The one about the crowns, he writes twice. On the first dawn of the new year, the whole court bows to the queen at once. Silla never bothered with that before. A law office opens beside the Secretariat. Every True Bone with a post now carries an ivory tablet. He holds it like a man who has been handed a live fish.
[42] ── SCENE: The Woven Ode ──
[43] ¶ The queen weaves the ode herself, at the loom she sits at when nobody is comparing. It takes her a season. When Bupmin comes to collect it, she does not let go of the bolt at once.
[44] Queen Jinduk: Tell him I wove it. / Not wrote. Wove. / …Unni could see the future. I can at least make it look nice.
[45] King Munmu: I’ll tell him, Your Highness.
[46] ¶ Bupmin sails west with it. The new emperor in Chang’an admires it extravagantly. He also reads the letter rolled up inside, which asks for the Baekje cities back.
[47] [POEM Ode to Great Peace (太平頌) [Queen Jinduk] (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Jindeok, yr. 4 (650), sixth month · cf. Jiu Tangshu bk. 199上 (止戈戎衣定)): Great Tang has opened its vast work; lofty, lofty, the imperial plan shines. / The spear is stilled and its might has settled all; letters are cultivated, heir to a hundred kings. / It rules as Heaven does and honours the falling rain; it orders all things and keeps their beauty within. / Its deep kindness keeps pace with sun and moon; its fortunes outrun the years of peace. / How bright, how bright the banners blaze; how loud, how loud the gongs and drums. / Outer tribes who defy its command are cut down by Heaven’s punishment. / Pure custom settles on the seen and the unseen; near and far vie to offer good omens. / The four seasons turn in tune like a jade candle; the seven lights wheel over ten thousand lands. / The holy peaks send down ministers; the emperor trusts the loyal and good. / The Three and the Five are made one virtue: shine on, sovereign of our Tang house!*]
[48] King Munmu: Father. The collar itches.
[49] King Muyeol: Everything new itches. / Wear it to the Council, and watch which uncles scratch.
[50] ── SCENE: Yamato ──
[51] ¶ That summer a Silla tribute ship puts in at a Yamato harbour, its envoys dressed in the new robes. The Yamato court takes one look at them and sends them home.
[52] Kose no Ōmi: If we do not strike Silla now, we will regret it later. / Fill the sea from our harbours to theirs with ships, bow to stern, and call them to account. It would be easy.
[53] ¶ The Yamato emperor does not fill the sea. His successors will remember the idea.
[54] ── SCENE: Sabi ──
[55] ¶ The emperor’s answer goes to Sabi first, because it is addressed to Sabi. Euija reads it aloud to the whole hall. He reads everything aloud, insults especially.
[56] King Euija: “Return the cities you took from Silla.” Ha! Listen to this, Gyebek. It gets better. / “If the king will not obey, We grant Bupmin’s request, and leave him to settle it with you in battle.” / In battle! The Son of Heaven writes me a whole scroll to say he’s staying home.
[57] Gyebek: Then it is only Silla.
[58] King Euija: Only Silla! Hear that? Heaven just counted my enemies for me. One! / Write back that we’re honoured. Then go and take another fort.
[59] Gyebek: …For now, one.
[60] ── SCENE: Surabol ──
[61] ¶ In Surabol, Jukji reads the copy that came home with Bupmin. He reads the battle line twice.
[62] Kim Jukji: He’ll let us fight them, my lord. / He doesn’t say he’ll fight with us.
[63] King Muyeol: No. / His father said that. In a gallery full of horses, with the lamp on the floor.
[64] ¶ **What happened to that promise? Two years back, the room is too warm, and a dying emperor has one more thing to say…!**
